This memorial is not made of stone; it has a pulse.
To see these two veteran actors together is a treat.
Janice Honeyman’s production has two really affectionate performances, laced with the melancholy of ageing and the fear of mortality.

The play is a compelling if cursory exploration of the legacy of Apartheid as expressed through the fast-flowering yet prickly rapport between a dying white South African actor and the elderly black male nurse who comes to tend to him.
It feels like theatre by old people, for old people.
A play about human dignity and outreach, it dignifies the West End, too.
It is not only the politics but also the attitudes of the men and the communities that they embody which are so richly drawn.
This terrific two-hander is currently berthed at the smallish Ambassadors.
Kunene and the King is made remarkably light on its feet by the plain human engagement of these two combatants.
Janice Honeyman’s direction excels in getting just such details right.
Kani in particular paints powerfully a picture of a man whose essential goodness and dignity hides a constant anger at all that has happened to him. He is wonderful to watch.
Despite all these good ingredients the play fails to grip, and feels repetitive.
The final scene in Kuni's house is a masterclass of pathos and physical comedy as they assert and seal their mutual respect and affection.
Yet for all this preachy, message-laden dialogue, I liked it.

cn.t: Critics find this apartheid-legacy two-hander warm and humane, praising Kani and Sher's performances, though some dismiss it as heavy-handed and overly earnest. The King Lear parallels resonate for most, but a few find the approach dated.
